draft.title: Showing through detail
card: Telling names a feeling directly: "Sam was nervous." Showing gives details and lets the reader work out the feeling for themselves.
Good details are specific and concrete. They can be seen, heard, touched or done, such as a clenched jaw, a dry mouth or a pen tapping on a desk.
The reader infers the feeling from the details. This draws them into the scene, and the feeling often seems stronger than a single named word.
A vague detail such as "she looked upset" is still telling. A showing detail is one you could picture, such as "she pressed her sleeve to her eyes".
draft.remember: Give the reader concrete details to picture, and let them infer the feeling.

a.q: Which sentence shows a character's fear through detail, instead of telling it?
opts: Her hand shook so hard the latch rattled on the gate
Mina was terrified of walking into the dark house
Mina felt very afraid as she stood at the door
Fear swept over Mina as she reached the front door
a.why: The shaking hand and rattling latch are concrete details the reader can picture, so they infer the fear. The other three name the feeling directly, even when they sound dramatic.
a.clue: Which sentence never names the feeling?

b.q: A student drafts: "Dad was disappointed in me." Which rewrite is the best example of showing?
opts: Dad set down the report card and stared at the window
Dad gave me a look that was clearly full of disappointment
Dad sighed and said he was upset about my marks
Dad looked sad and let down by what I had done
b.why: Setting down the card and staring away are specific actions the reader can picture and use to infer disappointment. The look "full of disappointment" is tempting, but it still names the feeling, so it tells.
b.clue: Look for an action you could picture, not a named emotion.

a.best: Her hand shook so hard the latch rattled on the gate

b.best: Dad set down the report card and stared at the window
